scene.title: Huawei|On Trial
scene.sub: United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. · E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 · verdict Nov 24, 2026

lines.say: Chapter one. The verdict.

The Justice Department's announcement lists what the jury convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries of. Conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud. Wire fraud. Bank fraud.

scene.title: What the jury convicted
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: Conspiracy to defraud the United States. Conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, and substantive violations of that law. And money laundering conspiracy.
Prosecutors said the defendants were Huawei Technologies, the Chinese parent company, plus Huawei Device, and two American subsidiaries, Futurewei Technologies and Huawei Device U.S.A.
lines.show: Prosecutors said the defendants were Huawei Technologies, the Chinese parent company, plus Huawei Device, and two American subsidiaries, Futurewei Technologies and Huawei Device USA.

scene.title: Four defendants
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: According to AFP, Huawei was convicted on ten of twelve criminal charges. The jury deliberated for five days, after more than sixty witnesses called by prosecutors, and fifteen called by the defense.
lines.show: According to AFP, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 criminal charges. The jury deliberated for five days, after more than 60 witnesses called by prosecutors, and 15 called by the defense.

scene.kicker: THE TRIAL · AS REPORTED BY AFP
scene.label: criminal charges: guilty
scene.src: IBTimes (Merin Rebecca Thomas), citing AFP, Nov 24, 2026

lines.say: Huawei was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy, and of conspiracy to obstruct justice. Racketeering is the charge that treats a company as a criminal enterprise. Before deliberations, the government had asked the judge for a modified instruction on how racketeering acts must be related to each other. The letters do not say whether the judge gave it.

scene.title: The racketeering instruction

scene.q: No person or company is above the law.

lines.say: The government told the judge this was not a trial of China, or of Iran. Before the jury was picked, the government wrote to the judge about prospective jurors who had answered questions on those topics.

scene.title: Who is on trial
scene.src: Government letter to Judge Donnelly, Aug 31, 2026 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 823)

lines.say: The government said, quote, the government of the People's Republic of China, the Chinese Communist Party, the government of Iran, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, are not on trial. The defendants were companies.

The case is older than most people realize. The indictment on the court docket today is the fourth superseding indictment, numbered S-4. An earlier one, the S-3, filed in February twenty twenty, named five companies and Huawei's chief financial officer. The one filed in April of this year names four companies.

lines.say: So what did Huawei do? The Justice Department's answer starts with a robot.

lines: What does the Justice Department|say it proved?
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: Chapter two. The robot.
The robot belonged to T-Mobile. Its name was Tappy. It tests how a phone's touch screen responds, by mimicking a human touch. The Justice Department says Tappy was a T-Mobile trade secret.

scene.title: T-Mobile’s robot, “Tappy”
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: The indictment does not name the company and the announcement does not cite the paragraph, but both describe a phone-testing robot taken from a lab. In May twenty twelve, it says, Huawei Device USA asked a U.S. wireless network operator to sell or license its phone-testing robot. The company declined.
lines.show: The indictment does not name the company and the announcement does not cite the paragraph, but both describe a phone-testing robot taken from a lab. In May 2012, it says, Huawei Device USA asked a U.S. wireless network operator to sell or license its phone-testing robot. The company declined.

scene.title: The robot was not for sale
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: Then, the indictment says, Huawei and Huawei Device began to build their own robot, and told Huawei's American employees to send them detailed information about the other company's technology.

The Justice Department says Huawei signed a nondisclosure agreement with T-Mobile, fully intending to violate it. And that Huawei employees in the United States sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China.

In May twenty thirteen, the indictment says, Huawei sent an engineer to the United States. He described the trip in his own words. Quote: go to the laboratory for reconnaissance and obtain measurement data.
lines.show: In May 2013, the indictment says, Huawei sent an engineer to the United States. He described the trip in his own words. Quote: "go to the [Company 5] laboratory for reconnaissance and obtain measurement data."

scene.title: “…for reconnaissance…”
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: Then came the arm. On May twenty-ninth, twenty thirteen, the indictment says, an employee surreptitiously placed a robot arm into a laptop bag, and removed it from the laboratory. The Justice Department's announcement says backpack. The photographs and measurements were emailed to engineers.
lines.show: Then came the arm. On May 29, 2013, the indictment says, an employee surreptitiously placed a robot arm into a laptop bag, and removed it from the laboratory. The Justice Department's announcement says backpack. The photographs and measurements were emailed to engineers.

scene.title: The robot arm
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: And when the other company noticed? The indictment says Huawei Device USA wrote an Investigation Report. It described the actions as isolated incidents, and one engineer's conduct as a moment of indiscretion.

scene.title: “Isolated incidents”
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: According to Global Investigations Review, Huawei's defense closing described the case as ordinary business activity and isolated employee misconduct. The jury convicted Huawei of conspiracy to steal trade secrets.

scene.kicker: THE DEFENSE · AS REPORTED BY GIR
scene.src: Global Investigations Review, Nov 18, 2026

lines.say: Chapter three. The code and the circuit board.

scene.title: The Code and the Circuit Board

lines.say: Tappy was one example. The Justice Department listed others it says were proved at trial. The first is Cisco. Prosecutors say Huawei copied the source code used on Cisco routers, which the announcement calls the crown jewel of Cisco technology.

scene.title: Cisco’s “crown jewel”
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: And in a poorly conceived effort to hide the theft, the announcement says, Huawei engineers left Cisco's own notes in the code. They referred to Cisco by its name written backwards. O, C, S, I, C.

scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: Then, the announcement says, Fujitsu. A Huawei employee was caught photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment. His badge claimed he worked for a company called Weihua, not Huawei.

scene.title: A badge that said “Weihua”
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: The indictment describes a July 2004 trade-show incident in Chicago, involving a company it calls Company 3 and does not name. A badge reading Weihua appears there too, but the announcement does not say it is the same incident. According to the indictment, Huawei told Reuters the man was a junior engineer who had never traveled to the United States before, and a resume he gave the U.S. government around 2012 described him as a senior R&D engineer.

scene.title: “A junior engineer…”
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: Then a circuit board. When CNEX, a U.S. technology company, would not collaborate with Huawei directly, the Justice Department says Huawei hired a university researcher to arrange it, without disclosing that he was acting for Huawei. He gave Huawei direct access to CNEX's proprietary hardware.

scene.caption: TRIAL EXHIBIT · CNEX SOLID-STATE DRIVE BOARD WITH WIRES ATTACHED BY HUAWEI ENGINEERS
scene.src: Trial exhibit released by the Justice Department with the verdict announcement (credit line: U.S. v. Huawei Technologies Co Ltd., Case No. 1:18-cr-00457)

lines.say: And Quintel, a U.S. antenna maker. Huawei received confidential information under a nondisclosure agreement. Almost immediately, the announcement says, Huawei filed a patent application for technology that included Quintel's idea, and attached a confidential Quintel slide to it.

scene.title: A patent filing with someone else’s slide
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: The indictment puts one figure on a different, unnamed company. It says that between about two thousand nine and two thousand sixteen, Huawei received about twenty-two million dollars in income from products that incorporated intellectual property it alleges was misappropriated from an antenna-technology company it calls Company 4.
lines.show: The indictment puts one figure on a different, unnamed company. It says that between about 2009 and 2016, Huawei received about $22 million in income from products that incorporated intellectual property it alleges was misappropriated from an antenna-technology company it calls Company 4.

scene.title: About $22 million
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: Prosecutors also alleged a policy. In twenty thirteen, the indictment says, Huawei launched a bonus program to reward employees who obtained confidential information from competitors. A group reviewed submissions and awarded monthly bonuses to the employees who provided the most valuable stolen information.
lines.show: Prosecutors also alleged a policy. In 2013, the indictment says, Huawei launched a bonus program to reward employees who obtained confidential information from competitors. A group reviewed submissions and awarded monthly bonuses to the employees who provided the most valuable stolen information.

scene.title: The bonus program
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: Huawei's response, according to AFP: the trade-secret disputes had been resolved as civil matters. The jury also heard fifteen defense witnesses.

scene.src: IBTimes (Merin Rebecca Thomas), citing AFP, Nov 24, 2026

lines.say: Chapter four. Skycom.
The verdict also covers Iran. The Justice Department says Huawei conducted its business in Iran under the name Skycom.

scene.title: “Skycom”
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: According to the announcement, Huawei repeatedly lied about that business. To banks, to journalists, and to the U.S. government. It said that it did not assist Iran's government, military or intelligence community. That it began restricting its Iran business in twenty eleven. That Skycom was a business partner, rather than a wholly owned subsidiary. And that Huawei complied with all applicable sanctions.
lines.show: According to the announcement, Huawei repeatedly lied about that business. To banks, to journalists, and to the U.S. government. It said that it did not assist Iran's government, military or intelligence community. That it began restricting its Iran business in 2011. That Skycom was a business partner, rather than a wholly owned subsidiary. And that Huawei complied with all applicable sanctions.

lines.say: The announcement says Huawei knew every one of those statements was materially false and misleading.

scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: The indictment describes the structure. It says Huawei operated Skycom as an unofficial subsidiary, to obtain otherwise prohibited American goods, technology and services, including banking services, while concealing the link to Huawei.

scene.title: An “unofficial subsidiary”
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: Internal documents, the indictment says, used code names for sanctioned countries. A-two meant Iran. A-nine meant North Korea. The United States and Canada got no code names.
lines.show: Internal documents, the indictment says, used code names for sanctioned countries. A2 meant Iran. A9 meant North Korea. The United States and Canada got no code names.

scene.title: “A2” = Iran
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: And what was at stake? According to the Justice Department, Huawei lied to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars, and access to dollar clearing services.

scene.title: “Billions of U.S. dollars”
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: The indictment gives one number. Between about twenty ten and twenty fourteen, it says, one bank and its American subsidiary cleared more than one hundred million dollars in transactions related to Skycom through the United States.
lines.show: The indictment gives one number. Between about 2010 and 2014, it says, one bank and its American subsidiary cleared more than $100 million in transactions related to Skycom through the United States.

scene.title: $100 million cleared through the U.S.
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: In two thousand thirteen, the indictment says, a Huawei executive presented a slide deck to a bank. It said Huawei operates in Iran in strict compliance with applicable laws, and that its engagement with Skycom is normal business cooperation. The indictment says: these statements were all false.
lines.show: In 2013, the indictment says, a Huawei executive presented a slide deck to a bank. It said Huawei operates in Iran in strict compliance with applicable laws, and that its engagement with Skycom is normal business cooperation. The indictment says: these statements were all false.

scene.title: The bank presentation
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: The announcement adds the part that is not about money. Testimony established, it says, that Huawei helped Iran monitor and censor internet access, and provided surveillance cameras that let the regime monitor protest activity.

scene.title: Surveillance and protest activity
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: The company also answered the press. The indictment says that in December twenty eleven, after a Wall Street Journal report, Huawei issued a press release saying it had, quote, no involvement in any type of monitoring and filtering activities.
lines.show: The company also answered the press. The indictment says that in December 2011, after a Wall Street Journal report, Huawei issued a press release saying it had, quote, "no involvement in any type of monitoring and filtering activities."

scene.title: Huawei’s December 2011 statement
scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: The indictment says that when Reuters reported in twenty twelve and twenty thirteen that Skycom had sold embargoed American goods to Iran, and that Huawei owned it, banks relied on Huawei's denials to decide whether to keep doing business with it. They kept doing business with it.
lines.show: The indictment says that when Reuters reported in 2012 and 2013 that Skycom had sold embargoed American goods to Iran, and that Huawei owned it, banks relied on Huawei's denials to decide whether to keep doing business with it. They kept doing business with it.

lines.say: The indictment alleges that Huawei told Congress something different. In twenty twelve, it says, a Huawei senior vice president testified before the House Intelligence Committee: quote, we have never provided any equipment to the Iranian government.
lines.show: The indictment alleges that Huawei told Congress something different. In 2012, it says, a Huawei senior vice president testified before the House Intelligence Committee: quote, "We have never provided any equipment to the Iranian government."

scene.src: Superseding Indictment S-4 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 689, filed Apr 17, 2026)

lines.say: The indictment says that testimony was false, and that Huawei's Iran business included providing goods and services to the Iranian government. The jury convicted Huawei on the sanctions, bank fraud and money laundering charges.
Chapter five. The last weeks.
The government's November fourteenth letter concerned the rebuttal evidence it planned to offer. The government wrote to the judge about the rebuttal evidence it planned to offer.
lines.show: The government's November 14 letter concerned the rebuttal evidence it planned to offer. The government wrote to the judge about the rebuttal evidence it planned to offer.

scene.title: Rebuttal evidence
scene.src: Government letter to Judge Donnelly, Nov 14, 2026 (United States v. Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., et al., E.D.N.Y. 18-cr-457 (AMD), Dkt. 954)

lines.say: The letter describes a recorded phone call in the government's case. In it, two Huawei employees, the letter says, discussed and coordinated a plan to send Chinese expatriate employees who worked in sensitive nations out of the jurisdiction of the United States.

The defense had told the jury another story, the letter says. That the expats were sent home because of headcount reductions and economic challenges at Huawei's American operations. The government said its rebuttal evidence would refute it.
The indictment also alleges that in April twenty eighteen, that Huawei made efforts to move an employee with knowledge of its Iran business to China, beyond the reach of the U.S. government.
lines.show: The indictment also alleges that in April 2018, that Huawei made efforts to move an employee with knowledge of its Iran business to China, beyond the reach of the U.S. government.

lines.say: Chapter six. What happens next.

Huawei has said it rejects the remaining allegations. According to AFP, it welcomed the acquittal on racketeering, said it would review the verdicts, and take legal action to defend its interests. Its attorney said the company was disappointed, and expects to appeal.

scene.kicker: HUAWEI'S RESPONSE · AS REPORTED BY AFP
scene.src: IBTimes (Merin Rebecca Thomas), citing AFP, Nov 24, 2026

lines.say: The sentencing is set for September fourteenth, twenty twenty-seven. The Justice Department says a federal district court judge will determine any sentence, and that the defendants face criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution. AFP reports that the amounts have not been determined.
lines.show: The sentencing is set for September 14, 2027. The Justice Department says a federal district court judge will determine any sentence, and that the defendants face criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution. AFP reports that the amounts have not been determined.

scene.title: Penalties still to come
scene.src: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, press release 26-1413 (Nov 24, 2026)

lines.say: The jury convicted on the trade-secret conspiracy, the bank fraud, the sanctions violations and the money laundering. The Justice Department says the robot arm and the Skycom name are among the evidence it proved at trial. The bank presentation is an allegation from the indictment. Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva of the Criminal Division said, quote, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception. According to AFP, Huawei rejects the remaining allegations.

scene.sub: Racketeering conspiracy: acquitted · Huawei's attorney expects to appeal · as reported by AFP

lines.say: A company can't be sent to prison. So what should a punishment for a company look like? A fine so large it changes how it does business? Tell us in the comments.
